#425. Nvidia Scandal Unleashes a Flood of AI-Generated Memes

The revelations surrounding Jensen Huang, who resigned from Nvidia over extramarital affairs, inspired social media posts using the very technology his company helped develop.

Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.

Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.

In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.

Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.

Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.

Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

#423. More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials

People with experimental brain implants are pushing for more recognition and respect.

Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.

“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.

“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”

#419. Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died

After years in elite police units, he drew scrutiny from human rights groups for selling arms and providing other services to unsavory governments. He was 80.

Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

#416. Building AI that can work across the enterprise

Moving AI beyond isolated pilots requires a strong data foundation, clear business outcomes, and governance built for enterprise scale.

For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys.

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys.Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we're still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI's value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It's becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can't simply be added into an enterprise's existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what's inside and how it's used.

Two words for you: conscious configuration.My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy.Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder.

Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation.

Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion.

Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack?

Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation.This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization.The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes.

Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we're seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What's the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well?

Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that's a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap.

What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn't recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start.

And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you're not building AI today, you're not standing still, you're falling behind at an accelerating rate.

Megan: Right. There's a real polarization there, isn't there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity?

Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it's a technology rollout.Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale.

Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation.

In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that's what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios.

And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps.

And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well.

Megan: Right. It's been really clear, isn't it, on what you're looking to achieve and what's worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten's framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously.The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction.Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what's the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three.

Megan: That's such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example.

Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that's why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it's very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side.

One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that's why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company's reality and not just in generic patterns.

And then, I think, the second element that's important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result.

The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that's why it's important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system.

And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable.

Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI's capability a little bit easier?

Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership.

SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP's industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement.

In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months.

What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What's hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations. That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel.

Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP's Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms?

Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars.

The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP's own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed.

Complimenting what Satinder said, it's really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don't cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together.

Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC.

With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that's part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform.

And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework.

And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they're integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire.

Megan: Fantastic. That's a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they've used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I'll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP's three pillar look like in production.

The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys' agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million.The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That's the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept.

Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what's your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP?

Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you're absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it's important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they're public models. Depending on the provider's policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk.

So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they're lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That's why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit.

And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical.

As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP.

Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack?

Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That's the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront.What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical.The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower.The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren't just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what's running, what it's consuming, and whether it's performing as expected. That's what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset.

And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle.

Megan: That's such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we've covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we've spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer?

Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak.Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs.On the technology front, I think there's still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we'll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there's an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable.And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future.

Megan: Which is, of course, what we're aiming for. And how about you, Satinder? What would you flag as a really exciting area of development?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think what excites me most is the shift from AI as productivity tool to AI as a decision-making partner. The most important evolution Thorsten's architecture makes possible. For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take.

The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That's not a dashboard. That's a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains.

What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP's prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for.

The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available.

So, the next frontier isn't that AI can do more work. It's that AI that understands your business well enough to help you make better decision. And that's where the greatest opportunity for SAP, Infosys, and our clients lies, convergence of systems of record with systems of intelligence.

Megan: Fantastic. Certainly, lots on the horizon to look forward to. Thank you both so much for joining us today.That was Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America at SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.

That's it for this episode of Business Lab. I'm your host, Megan Tatum. I'm a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website, thetechnologyreview.com.This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you'll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thank you so much for listening. Goodbye.

#413. Outlook Went Down? Microsoft May Owe You Money

Rest assured that while Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services were flatlining this week, the company’s billing operations were still firing on all cylinders. Copilot can’t run on air alone, after all. It needs cash.

The silver lining is that, in the light of our global recovery from one of the most debilitating tech outages in recent memory, Microsoft now owes you compensation. And depending on the size of your operation and the degree to which you rely on Microsoft products, the payout could be substantial.

If you have a business relationship with Microsoft—a subscription to a Microsoft 365 Business plan, email hosted on Microsoft Exchange, or perhaps a Teams Premium tier—that relationship is governed by reams of documentation, among them being a service level agreement.

Service level agreements, or SLAs, are old hat to large enterprises, who use them to hold service providers like web hosts and email services accountable, ensuring they stay online and operational—and they are often in the realm of demanding 99.99 percent reliability or higher, as is the default promise with Microsoft Azure. If a provider fails to hit the promised availability level, the customer is due a refund (or credit toward next month’s bill, at least).

But SLAs don’t apply only to the Fortune 500. If you have a business account with Microsoft, no matter how small it is, your service is also governed by these promises. And now, Microsoft owes you money.

“Business account” is the key phrase in the above, mind you. If you have a Microsoft 365 Family plan or any other individual or personal plan, you are probably out of luck. Outlook could go offline for a month and you wouldn’t be entitled to anything aside from a series of pointed Facebook posts.

The consumer Microsoft Services Agreement states that individual users can get refunds or credits at Microsoft’s “sole discretion,” but it doesn’t even mention SLAs and promises nothing in the way of uptime. In other words, if your email system wasn’t working for you on November 12, you can ask for money back, but your odds of receiving anything are low.

Business users are in a much more advantageous position, though Microsoft doesn’t exactly go out of its way to guide you through the refund process. SLA refunds are not automatic. You have to request them for each incident, and the process is hardly straightforward.

To figure out what you’re owed, start by taking a look at the SLA for Microsoft’s Online Services. (This is different than the above consumer Microsoft Services Agreement.) It’s more than 53,000 words long, and quite repetitive, but I’ll distill the key points for you here.

While many of the promised service levels are identical, start by double-checking the specific Microsoft products you use, as the SLA is broken down by product. A search for “Exchange Online” reveals everything you need to know, in surprisingly plain English.

Downtime is defined as “any period of time when users are unable to send or receive email with Outlook Web Access.”

Uptime Percentage is calculated by a simple formula: Subtract the minutes of downtime from your total User Minutes, then divide the result by your total User Minutes. Take that result and multiply it by 100.

“Downtime is measured in user-minutes; that is, for each Applicable Period, Downtime is the sum of the length (in minutes) of each Incident that occurs during that Applicable Period multiplied by the number of users impacted by that Incident.”

User minutes is the total number of minutes in the billing cycle; typically 30 days.

If the calculated uptime percentage falls below 99.9 percent, you are entitled to credit (not a cash refund) under the following terms:

If we assume the outage lasted about 18 hours for you, that equates to a 2.5 percent downtime percentage or a 97.5 percent uptime percentage for a 30-day billing cycle. And that puts you squarely in 50 percent service credit territory.

While Microsoft is transparent about what you are owed, it has less to say about what you have to do to receive it.

The SLA simply states that “in order for Microsoft to consider a claim, you must submit the claim to customer support at Microsoft Corporation including all information necessary for Microsoft to validate the claim.” You are also directed to supply the following:

(i) a detailed description of the Incident; (ii) information regarding the time and duration of downtime; (iii) affected resource names; (iv) the number and location(s) of affected users; and (v) a description of errors that occurred during the incident.

That’s a lot of information, but Microsoft likely does not need much in the way of (i) , (ii), or (v) to validate this global incident. You will need to supply the name of your “affected resource” and how many users were impacted. For the sake of completeness, include in your message the codes for outages for Exchange (EX1550543), Outlook (MO1550821), and Teams (TM1550488) as relevant to your business.

I also did the math on what my various Microsoft subscriptions cost. I only have two, Exchange Online and Microsoft 365 Business Standard, both of which were impacted by the outage. Total price of my last bill: $24.88. Thus, total credit due: $12.44. That may barely be beer money for me, but a company of 100 people will likely be owed over $1,000. If you don’t have these numbers handy, you’ll find them under Billing > Bills & Payments in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center.

With that information collected, then what? Microsoft simply directs you to file a claim with customer service, so that’s exactly what I did. In the same Admin Center, the method to file an email service request is a little tricky. It’s not in the left-hand navigation but rather can be found on the bottom right of the screen. Click the headset icon, which expands to reveal “Help & support.” This will default you to Microsoft’s AI chatbot. Within this page, click the headset icon at the top of the screen, which will take you to a “Contact support” page. Choose Email from this screen, and fill in the form with the information you’ve collected.

When reached for comment, Microsoft said that for the fastest service, customers should file their request with this exact title in their service request:

“SLA Credit Service Incidents: EX1550543/MO1550821”

That title includes the codes for the Exchange and Outlook outages.

Your submission should garner a quick response that includes a case-number tracking ID. I filed for compensation on Friday and haven’t gotten any response yet other than a confirmation of receipt. But considering that 12 principle-filled dollars are on the line, you can bet I’ll be tracking it closely.

As a final note: Be aware that claims must be submitted by the end of the month following the outage. So you have until December 31, 2026, to file your claim for the November 12 incident.

When I reached out to Microsoft for comment on this story, a PR rep said she would “let me know if the company has anything to share,” while offering the same statement you have probably seen too many times already: “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.”

Now we’ll see how seriously it takes the refund process.

Update, Saturday, November 14, at 2 pm: This story was updated to include the additional comment from Microsoft about how customers should title their credit request emails.

#411. Howard Lutnick Took Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew

Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.

Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region.Credit...Doug Mills/The New York Times

By Ana SwansonTripp MickleMaggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan

Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.

There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.

The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.

The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.

The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.

Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Yesterday was a good day for SpaceX and Elon Musk, and a banner day in the history of man's quest for the stars.

Not only did the launch of Starship, the largest interplantery rocket in the SpaceX fleet, standing over 400 feet tall and weighing over 5,000 tons, go off without a hitch from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas, but the vessel successfully delivered its payload of 26 Starlink V3 satellites over the course of its 22.5-hour mission, according to reporting from CNN, while orbiting the Earth 14 times.

But the real sticking point was always going to be the landing, where the SpaceX team attempted to prove their "reusable" rocket theory by successfully catching the falling Starship with some well-timed rocket boosters and incredible feats of engineering. The catch has been attempted a few times before on prior missions, successfully for the Super Heavy Booster on three occasions, but yesterday marked the first time the actual Starship was caught by the company's giant mechanical arms.

Understandably elated, Musk took to X, the social media site formerly known as Twitter, to share his incredible POV from atop the tower, shortly after the Starship catch:

Because journalists and bystanders were relegated to a safe watch site far away from the Starship catch site, most of the photos and footage of the catch struggles to convey the sheer size of the spaceship, but Musk's perspective gives a better sense of the scale of the ship and, therefore, the incredible challenge of executing a soft landing.

And for a better sense of how incredible the maneuver itself was, check out this time-lapse shot also shared by Musk:

If you missed the high drama of this most recent launch and landing, no worries: the next SpaceX mission, USSF-317, is around the corner.

#407. Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029

Climate action has stalled for five years as fossil fuel development keeps growing.

ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.

Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.

“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”

The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the UN “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.

“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”

Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

“Our message is a stark one,” Heck said. “Collective government action on climate change has stalled for the fifth consecutive year.” Efforts to speed up the shift away from fossil fuels have been negated by new oil and gas drilling projects and governments that are “delaying, weakening or rolling back their climate policies.”

Even under the most optimistic scenario, assuming full implementation of existing policies and promises, global temperatures would rise 3.4° Fahrenheit above preindustrial levels by 2100, an increase climate scientists consider extremely dangerous.

While there has been progress on developing renewable energy sources, the “brutal truth is that these positive developments have not yet added up to bend the curve fast enough,” said Niklas Höhne, a researcher with The New Climate Institute. Developing new oil and gas projects is a bit like discovering your food is burning and then turning up the stove instead of turning it off, he added.

Getting into the specifics of the current negotiations at COP31 surrounding global renewable goals, he noted that conference co-hosts Turkey and Australia have so far opposed including the word “clean” in connection with electrification targets.

“It’s very hard to understand, and the only explanation I can think of is their interest in fossil fuels,” Höhne said.

Australia is one of the world’s biggest coal exporters, and Turkey is a major coal consumer, with its power sector still highly dependent on the most climate-damaging fossil fuel. Even as they host this year’s climate conference, neither country has offered any specific plans to transition away from fossil fuels.

Bill Hare, the CEO of Climate Analytics, called out wealthy, developed countries for their lack of leadership on climate action, noting that European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen failed to mention anything about transitioning away from fossil fuels during her speech this week at COP31.

“Governments … at this COP have a stark choice,” Hare said. If they continue supporting fossil fuels, “it would consign humanity and our ecosystems to insurmountable economic damage and irretrievable loss.”

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

#406. These ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Have Lost Their Dark Matter

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.

Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.

But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses—using the motions of their stars as a proxy—the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?

A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter—their gas and dust—swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three new galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.

It’s a convincing explanation for many experts—one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.

Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.

These bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark-matter-lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars—and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.

That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji said.

What, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s—and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin—cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a stealthy type of neutrino? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs? Some have even opined that it could be primordial black holes as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.

“We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” said Daniel Whiteson, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter is matter.”

Dark matter, which makes up 27 percent of the universe—and 85 percent of all matter—interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.

“You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” said Chamkaur Ghag, a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding says no.”

So when DF2 was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawaii to track the motions of those stars to estimate the galaxy's total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark-matter-deficient galaxy ever spotted.

In 2019, they observed DF4, another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists announced that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.

That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce around an origin story.

Dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.

“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said Aaron Romanowsky, an astronomer at San Jose State University.

Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.

It’s reminiscent of the Bullet Cluster, two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter got torn asunder during the collision.

Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.

Kinwah Wu, a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.

Stacy McGaugh, an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he said. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.

“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.

Most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.

That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist Mordehai Milgrom. “MOND says: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.

MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull—for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances—the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.

Dark matter has long been the favored theory for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a significant blow in 2015 when the US-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves—ripples in the fabric of the universe—for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.

DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji said.

“I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson said. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”

The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.

#405. John Mulaney roasts dumbass Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in SNL monologue: No one likes him

John Mulaney spent a solid chunk of his seventh Saturday Night Live monologue going nuclear on US Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The bit began with Mulaney talking about hosting his children's friends, and how one child always seems to have an old man voice, not unlike Kennedy's.

From there, Mulaney launched into a full-on impression of Kennedy, rasping, "Stop the science! Robitussin, when taken during menstruation, will cause telekinesis."

Mulaney then talked about how "no one likes [Kennedy] anymore," not even his right-wing friends who used to approve of Kennedy.

"You dumbass, your thing can't be the measles," Mulaney said. "That can't be your project, giving people the measles."

After riffing on Kennedy's poor health track record and his inability to live up to his father's legacy, Mulaney explained that he knew Kennedy during his early days in New York ("He wasn't hard to know"). He skewered everything from his work as an environmental lawyer to his organization Riverkeeper, which was in charge of keeping the Hudson River — "whose native fish is tied-off used condom" — clean.

Mulaney recalled how he and other comedians would perform at the annual Riverkeeper benefit, and how he once received a garbled voicemail from Kennedy thanking him for the performance.

While Mulaney described bombing at the benefit, this SNL monologue had the opposite effect. Watch the full set above. #403. We Asked Vogue, GQ, and a Pro Stylist to Kill Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket

Jensen Huang’s midlife-crisis makeover hasn’t helped the Nvidia CEO’s image this week. In a matter of days, Huang’s questionable sartorial leanings have shifted wildly from wannabe cool Harley dad to low-down leather Lothario. Fashion moves fast, but even in the style world, this is a breakneck volte-face.

As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.

This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less. We’ve charted the menacing glow-up of tech bros before, but merely observing the worrying trend back in 2025 is clearly no longer enough. It’s time to roll up our Armani sleeves and help.

“Tech bros were total nerds before," says Karen Clarkson, a professional stylist whose clients have included Nike, Google, Apple, Calvin Klein, and Vivienne Westwood. "Fashion didn’t touch their lives at all. They didn’t have style.” Pictures of Huang’s pre-biker fashion-vacuum days certainly bear this out. “Then, like [Jeff] Bezos, they all stepped up. And there’s a rivalry that’s come with that, whether it’s the fashion makeover, the grooming, the skin treatments, or gym regimen. Now we have Mark Zuckerberg in the front row at Prada.”

Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 1! (clockwise from top left): Giorgio Armani long-sleeved cashmere polo, $1,695; Lemaire workwear jacket, $1,050; The Row Nesper pant, $1,250; Giorgio Armani leather slippers, $1,850; Speciale cotton-mix stripe shirt; £295.

As a man clearly in dress distress, where better to start than with Murray Clark, head of editorial at British GQ. Controversially, Clark has a radical notion that Huang should keep clothing matters as they are. “I’d argue that Jensen Huang stays exactly how he is because this is who he is—a coiffed, leather-jacket wearing, mistake-making middle-aged man for all the world to see.”

Before publicly admitting on Sunday to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence says is also a Chinese spy, in 2024, Huang confessed onstage that his wife, Lori, suggested and chose his biker outfits for him because he found most other fabrics “itchy.”

If Jensen keeps his jackets (he apparently owns 30 to 40), Clarkson thinks that Huang might even find himself on the catwalk. “If he wants to go down that route, then for sure Demna [Gucci’s creative director] would have him walking in his next show in Milan,” she says. “But he’s very Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Terminator with his black leathers, which is a bit close to the bone, really, with AI and that humanity is potentially doomed. I don’t know if he’s wise to lean into Arnie too heavily.”

Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 2! (clockwise from top left): The Row Vana jacket, $12,000; Speciale lambswool crew, £435; The Row Victor shirt, $1,290; Lemaire Rail Belt, $320; John Lobb City II New Standard shoes, $1,878; The Row Paulo corduroy pant, $1,590.

Let’s get some sage advice, then, from Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial at British Vogue. “If I were styling Jensen Huang, I’d advise him to cleanse the palate entirely, ditch the rock and roll shrunken leather jackets for something more somber,” Nnadi says. “A collared Oxford shirt and a navy or gray crewneck jumper would do the trick and wouldn’t read as aggressively corporate as a traditional suit. The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’”

Clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy. So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.

“He could take a leaf out of Harry Styles’ dress down codes and check The Row for minimal looks,” Clarkson says. “A Lemaire workwear jacket is also a good vibe. It shows he’s willing to put in the work to win back his family. Also, since he’s spoken about feeling itchy, maybe he should repent a bit and wear lambswool instead of cashmere.”

Jensen Huang's Banished Biker Look 3! (clockwise from top left): Paul Smith Ripstop field jacket, $1,025; Brunello Cucinelli alpaca-blend sweater, $3,400; The Row Sue pant, $2,300; Paul Smith Garson shoes, $475.

Asking Clarkson to step away from her celebrity clients for a moment to perform a hasty hypothetical make under (or glow down?) for Huang, she has very kindly put together three outfits that I think we can all agree give off considerably fewer bad-egg biker vibes with pieces from Paul Smith, The Row, Lemaire, Giorgio Armani, Brunello Cucinelli, and more. If you’re lucky enough to have a budget to match Huang's, we’ve added links to the individual pieces in the captions under each “look.”

“There’s been a lot of tight-fitted leather jackets that just about cover his biceps, which always feels like he’s looking to lure his next lover or like he’s just whizzed off on his Ducati to have a quick lunchtime visit with his mistress,” says Clarkson. “That’s not the vibe you want to go before Congress with.” For the Hill, she suggests Huang go for a Nehru collar that “feels a bit more buttoned up.”

Giorgio Armani's Spring-Summer 2027 show in Milan.

However, because Huang’s existing look is so strong, Clarkson advises that changing it too quickly will not only draw an enormous amount of commentary but even more memes. “Little steps, not a full overnight makeover. That’s why he should perhaps keep the leather jacket, something like a suede blouson instead of the biker,” she says, adding that the black jeans should be ditched in favor of proper pants.

“He could do a tie as well—a bit more apologetic, a bit more formal, a bit more respectful. So a brown leather jacket with a tie and a shirt—so then it’s a segue into a new direction,” Clarkson says, citing Giorgio Armani’s June Milan collection as ideal inspiration.

However, Clarkson says credit must ultimately go to Lori Huang, Jensen’s wife of 41 years. “She did a brilliant job. If anyone comes out of this as a winner, it’s her. She could rebrand as a Hollywood stylist at this point because she’s done a great job of creating an identity for her husband. Almost too good because it’s attracted too many women. Still, she could step away with a really great divorce settlement and a whole new career.”
